title: Purchase Price Mechanics
summary: Purchase Price Mechanics explain how enterprise value becomes actual equity proceeds after debt, cash, working capital, and deal-specific adjustments.
definition: Purchase price mechanics are the transaction rules that convert headline valuation into final cash paid to sellers and capital required from buyers.
whyItMatters: PE operators need this because value can move materially through cash-free debt-free adjustments, net working capital pegs, debt-like items, rollover equity, earnouts, and seller notes.
example: A company sold for $300M enterprise value may deliver far lower seller proceeds after debt payoff, working capital shortfall, transaction expenses, and rollover equity.

graph TD
  A[Enterprise Value] --> B[Minus Debt and Debt-Like Items]
  A --> C[Plus Cash]
  A --> D[Working Capital Adjustment]
  B --> E[Equity Value]
  C --> E
  D --> E
  E --> F[Seller Proceeds]

articleSections.title: Build the Enterprise-Value-to-Equity-Value Bridge
body: Purchase price mechanics convert an agreed enterprise value into equity value and then into cash delivered to each seller. Enterprise value prices the operating business independent of financing. The equity bridge adds cash that the seller retains economically, subtracts funded debt and agreed debt-like obligations, and adjusts for closing net working capital relative to a normalized peg. A second proceeds waterfall then separates equity value from cash at closing by deducting seller expenses, escrow or holdback funding, and rollover equity while identifying contingent consideration. Keeping these two bridges distinct prevents a financing or timing item from being mistaken for a valuation adjustment.

Consider a $300 million enterprise value. Add $8 million of eligible cash, subtract $72 million of funded debt and $9 million of debt-like items, and subtract a $4 million working-capital shortfall: closing equity value is $223 million. From that amount, deduct $6 million of seller transaction expenses, fund a $5 million indemnity escrow, and convert $30 million into rollover equity. Cash paid to sellers at closing is therefore $182 million. Economic proceeds are $217 million including the escrow, or $212 million when only closing cash and rollover equity are counted; the bridge must never present $300 million as immediately distributable proceeds.

Ownership starts before exclusivity. The deal lead owns the commercial terms and integrated bridge; the CFO or controller owns source schedules and closing estimates; legal counsel owns definitions in the purchase agreement; tax advisers own tax-specific liabilities; and the operating partner challenges whether the balance sheet delivered at close can support the plan. A weekly bridge should become daily during the final week. Each version shows source date, preparer, reviewer, unresolved classifications, sensitivity, and the party bearing the item. The signing gate is a fully defined formula; the funding gate is a reconciled funds-flow statement tied to payoff letters and bank instructions.
articleSections.callout: A credible price has two reconciled views: enterprise value to equity value, then equity value to cash, rollover, escrow, and contingent proceeds.

articleSections.title: Define Cash, Debt, and Debt-Like Items Before They Become Disputes
body: Cash-free, debt-free pricing sounds simple but depends on definitions. Eligible cash may exclude trapped foreign balances, restricted cash, customer funds, minimum operating cash, uncleared receipts, or amounts needed to cover outstanding checks. Funded debt typically includes revolvers, term loans, accrued interest, and breakage costs supported by lender payoff letters. The close process should map every general-ledger account to cash, debt, debt-like, working capital, or excluded status, with no account appearing in two categories. The governing principle is economic responsibility: an obligation generated before close should not silently consume the buyer's post-close cash.

Debt-like treatment is negotiated because many liabilities sit outside formal borrowings. Common candidates include transaction bonuses, unpaid change-of-control payments, accrued owner compensation, deferred payroll taxes, tax liabilities for pre-close periods, underfunded pensions, unpaid capital expenditure, litigation settlements, and lease termination obligations. Deferred revenue and customer deposits require more care: the liability may be working capital, debt-like, or excluded depending on whether the associated delivery cost remains with the buyer and how the peg was built. A label is not analysis. The schedule should quantify the remaining cash burden and confirm that the same burden is not already captured in normalized working capital or EBITDA.

A classification committee comprising finance, legal, tax, and the deal team should meet weekly from the first balance-sheet review. Each disputed line receives an amount, agreement reference, economic rationale, counterparty position, evidence, decision owner, and settlement range. Escalation thresholds should be explicit: the CFO can clear factual reconciliations, counsel can confirm drafting, but only the authorized deal principal can trade price or risk. Failure modes include double counting unpaid bonuses in both debt-like items and working capital, adding restricted cash, ignoring accrued interest through the funding date, and accepting estimated debt without payoff letters. The closing condition is a zero-duplicate account map tied to the latest trial balance.

articleSections.title: Set a Normalized Net Working Capital Peg
body: The net working capital adjustment is meant to deliver the operating business with a normal level of short-term capital, not to reprice ordinary seasonality after close. The parties first define included current assets and liabilities, then calculate historical balances using consistent accounting policies. A trailing-twelve-month average may be a starting point, but growth, seasonality, acquisitions, unusual payment timing, aging quality, and changing revenue mix can make a simple average wrong. The peg should represent the capital required to operate at the closing scale through the next normal cash cycle, supported by monthly and, where volatility warrants, weekly data.

Suppose included receivables are $38 million, inventory $24 million, and included current liabilities $32 million at close, producing $30 million of closing net working capital. If the negotiated peg is $34 million, the seller receives a $4 million downward adjustment. That amount reconciles to the enterprise-to-equity bridge above. If $3 million of overdue payables has already been classified as debt-like, those payables must be removed from the working-capital calculation or the seller would be charged twice. Likewise, an obsolete inventory reserve must follow the agreement's accounting hierarchy rather than being introduced opportunistically in the closing statement.

The controller owns the monthly schedule, aging tie-outs, and policy consistency; the commercial and operations teams validate seasonality, customer behavior, procurement cycles, and inventory requirements; and the deal team owns the negotiated peg. Review gates include reconciliation to audited or reviewed financials, a quality screen for aged receivables and obsolete stock, and a forecast showing that the delivered balance supports at least one normal operating cycle. Failure modes include cherry-picking low months, mixing gross and net balances, changing reserves at close, treating growth-funded working capital as excess, and letting a working-capital improvement initiative reduce the peg before the buyer has actually earned the improvement.

articleSections.title: Run Closing Accounts, Funds Flow, and Disputes as Controlled Processes
body: Most agreements use either locked-box economics or completion accounts. Under completion accounts, the seller delivers an estimated closing statement before funding, the buyer prepares a post-close statement within a defined period, the seller reviews it, and unresolved accounting disputes may go to an independent accountant. The agreement must establish definitions, an accounting hierarchy, consistent-practice rules, access rights, deadlines, materiality or de minimis terms, and the accountant's authority. Otherwise, a mechanical true-up becomes a second negotiation over valuation. The independent accountant should resolve submitted accounting items, not rewrite commercial terms that the parties failed to settle.

The funds-flow statement operationalizes the economics. It ties purchase price, debt payoffs, transaction expenses, escrow deposits, management payments, rollover subscriptions, tax withholding, and wire instructions to a single control total. Treasury verifies beneficiaries through an independent callback, counsel checks authorization and payoff conditions, and finance ties the bridge to the closing balance sheet. Version control matters because a late debt draw, fee invoice, or exercise payment can change dozens of allocations. The funding gate requires equal sources and uses, signed payoff letters, validated bank details, approved calculations, and an audit trail showing who changed each amount.

Dispute prevention is cheaper than dispute resolution. Before signing, both parties should calculate a sample statement from the same historical month and compare classifications. Before close, they should maintain a joint issues list and reserve negotiated terms for genuine judgment rather than arithmetic cleanup. After close, the buyer should preserve access to the close ledger and avoid operational changes that obscure the measurement period. Typical failures are missed notice deadlines, inconsistent reserve methods, unsupported management estimates, and disputes framed in legal language without a quantified schedule. An effective process narrows each challenge to account, amount, evidence, agreement clause, and requested correction.

articleSections.title: Prepare Operations for Day One and Protect Proceeds Certainty
body: Purchase price mechanics are not solely a legal or finance exercise because the delivered balance sheet determines Day One resilience. The operating partner should test whether cash on hand, revolving capacity, receivable collections, inventory, supplier terms, payroll timing, and planned capex can support the first thirteen weeks. If eligible cash is swept to the seller and working capital equals the peg but the business still faces a seasonal liquidity trough, the underwriting has missed an operating funding need. A thirteen-week cash forecast should therefore reconcile opening balances to the purchase agreement and financing model before funding.

Seller proceeds certainty also depends on the instruments used to bridge value. Rollover equity is ownership, not cash; escrow is delayed and at risk; an earnout depends on definitions and future performance; and a seller note adds credit and subordination exposure. In the $300 million example, the seller should understand the $182 million closing cash, $30 million rollover, $5 million escrow, and any contingent amount as separate risk buckets. Allocation waterfalls then account for option exercises, management pools, preferred rights, and tax withholding. The company cap table, funds flow, and equity-value bridge must produce the same total before anyone approves wires.

At underwriting, every dollar classified as debt-like or working-capital shortfall increases the buyer's effective entry cost if it was not reflected in the bid; every required liquidity reserve affects debt capacity and equity funding. During ownership, disciplined closing schedules become the baseline for cash conversion and balance-sheet controls. At exit, clean account maps, consistent policies, accurate monthly closes, and a defendable peg shorten diligence and reduce the chance of a last-minute proceeds haircut. The board should review unresolved purchase-account items at close, monthly until settlement, and again during exit readiness so temporary disputes do not become permanent leakage.
